displayQuote: It may be dangerous to be America's enemy, but to be America's friend is fatal

meta.title: Who really said "It may be dangerous to be America's enemy"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Henry Kissinger really said it, in November 1968 — but as the tail of an if-then sentence about South Vietnam, recorded by William F. Buckley Jr. in 1974. Quoted alone it becomes a verdict; in full it is a warning about one specific coup.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It may be dangerous to be America's enemy'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Kissinger, November 1968 — but the famous line is the 'then' half of a conditional about Nguyen Van Thieu. The truncation turns a prediction into a law of nature.

answer.label: Kissinger — but it is half of a sentence
answer.authorDates: 1923–2023 · US National Security Adviser and Secretary of State
answer.sourceLine: He really did say it, in November 1968, in the weeks between Nixon’s election and his inauguration — but not as a standalone judgment. It is the closing clause of a conditional: if the South Vietnamese president Nguyen Van Thieu were deposed as Ngo Dinh Diem had been in 1963, then the world would conclude this. The record is William F. Buckley Jr., who set the remark down in United Nations Journal: A Delegate’s Odyssey (Putnam, 1974), pp. 56–57. That is a named witness publishing six years later, not a transcript — which is why we file it as attributed rather than verified.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Nixon should be told that it is probably an objective of Clifford to depose Thieu before Nixon is inaugurated. Word should be gotten to Nixon that if Thieu meets the same fate as Diem, the word will go out to the nations of the world that it may be dangerous to be America's enemy, but to be America's friend is fatal.
trail: The setting is the interregnum of November 1968. Nixon had won; Lyndon Johnson was still president; the Paris talks were stuck on whether Saigon would come to the table. Kissinger, not yet in office, was talking to people around the incoming administration.

Buckley records the remark as a message meant to be passed on — Nixon should be told… word should be gotten to Nixon. Read that way, the famous line is not Kissinger’s view of America. It is his prediction of what other governments would conclude if Washington let a second allied leader be overthrown the citation trail ↗.

The two names carry the whole argument. Ngo Dinh Diem, president of South Vietnam, was overthrown and killed in a 1963 coup that the United States had encouraged. Nguyen Van Thieu was his eventual successor, and Clark Clifford was Johnson’s Defense Secretary. Kissinger’s point was that doing it twice would be noticed.

The earliest print appearance anyone has located is Buckley’s 1974 book. English Wikiquote files the line under Attributed for exactly that reason: the source is a reputable eyewitness account, not a document from Kissinger’s own hand Wikiquote ↗.

We have found no instance of Kissinger confirming or repeating the sentence himself in the fifty-five years he lived afterwards, and no contemporaneous memo of the conversation. If one exists, we have not seen it — and we are not going to invent a citation to close the gap.
source.excerptNote: The full passage as Buckley records it. Everything before the last twenty words is what the truncation removes: a named policy (Clifford's), a named person (Thieu), a named precedent (Diem) and an 'if'. What survives sounds like a permanent truth about American friendship. What he actually said was a forecast about one coup that had not happened yet.

author.name: Henry Kissinger
author.heading: About Henry Kissinger
author.metaLine: 1923–2023 · US National Security Adviser and Secretary of State
author.bio: Henry Kissinger (1923–2023) was born in Bavaria, fled Nazi Germany as a teenager, and became the most quoted — and most argued-about — American diplomat of the twentieth century, running foreign policy for Nixon and Ford and sharing the 1973 Nobel Peace Prize. He spoke in exactly this register: cold, conditional, structured as a prediction about how other capitals would read a move. That style is what makes him so easy to misquote. Strip the ‘if’ from a Kissinger sentence and you are left with something that sounds like a law of history, which is rarely what he meant and always what travels.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong here
misattribution.intro: The authorship is not in doubt. What goes wrong is everything around it — where the sentence starts, what year it is given, and what kind of statement it is taken to be.

items.why: The line is the ‘then’ of an if-then. He said the world would conclude this if Thieu were deposed as Diem had been. Quoted alone it reads as his settled opinion that American friendship kills — a much larger claim, and not the one he made the full passage ↗.

You will see ‘to be an enemy of America can be dangerous, but to be a friend is fatal’, and George F. Will’s 2002 version, ‘although it is dangerous to be America’s enemy, it can be lethal to be America’s friend.’ Buckley’s text is the one to quote.

Everything descends from one named source publishing six years after the fact. Buckley was well placed and specific, and nobody has ever contested it — but there is no transcript, no memo and no confirmation from Kissinger. That is strong attribution, not documentary proof.
It is regularly quoted as something Secretary of State Kissinger said. In November 1968 he held no office at all — he was two months from being named National Security Adviser.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Kissinger, November 1968, recorded by William F. Buckley Jr. in 1974 — but as the closing clause of a conditional about Nguyen Van Thieu, not as a general verdict on American friendship the sourcing ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It gets quoted every time an American ally is left exposed — Saigon, Kabul, the Kurds, Kyiv — because it says the quiet part with a shrug, and because it comes from the man who ran the policy rather than from someone protesting it. A confession beats an accusation every time.

The irony is that the full sentence is an argument against abandoning an ally. Kissinger was warning what it would cost the United States if Thieu went the way of Diem. The line survives as an indictment of American loyalty; he offered it as a reason to keep faith.
context.detailsSummary: The two names in the sentence
detailsBody: Ngo Dinh Diem: president of South Vietnam, overthrown and killed in a November 1963 coup that Washington had encouraged. The precedent Kissinger is pointing at.
Nguyen Van Thieu: his eventual successor, in office 1967-1975, and in November 1968 refusing to join the Paris talks.
Clark Clifford: Johnson's Secretary of Defense, whose objective Kissinger takes to be removing Thieu before Nixon was sworn in.
The whole remark is a message for the incoming administration, not a public statement — which is part of why the only record of it is a friend's memoir six years later.
Thieu did survive until 1975. Saigon fell anyway, and the line has been quoted about it ever since.
context.pull: He was not saying American friendship kills. He was saying: do not let the world start believing that.
